concepts.name: Classification of Migration: Types and Typologies
key_dimensions: Internal vs. International migration — definitional boundaries and overlap (e.g., cross-border tribal movements)
Voluntary vs. Forced migration — the grey zone (economic compulsion vs. genuine voluntarism)
Temporary, seasonal, circular, and permanent migration — distinctions and real-world examples from India
UPSC trap: Circular migration is NOT the same as seasonal migration — distinguish by intent and return pattern

concepts.name: Push and Pull Factors of Migration
key_dimensions: Classic Lee's Migration Theory — origin push, destination pull, intervening obstacles, personal factors
Distinguishing economic push (unemployment, low wages) from non-economic push (conflict, disaster, climate)
Pull factors in Indian context: urban employment, education, better infrastructure — city-specific examples
UPSC trap: 'Intervening obstacles' are often ignored — distance, cost, language, legal barriers are obstacles, not push factors

concepts.name: Rural-to-Urban Migration in India: Patterns and Drivers
key_dimensions: Census data trends — net migration flows, top origin and destination states (UP, Bihar → Maharashtra, Delhi, Gujarat)
Role of agrarian distress, fragmented landholdings, and monsoon dependency as structural push factors
Difference between distress migration and aspiration migration — policy implications of each
UPSC trap: Rural-urban migration does NOT always mean permanent settlement — most is circular/seasonal

concepts.name: Ravenstein's Laws of Migration: Applicability and Limitations
key_dimensions: Core laws — short-distance dominance, step migration, urban absorption, gender differentials, counter-streams
Validity in contemporary India — step migration visible (village → town → city) vs. direct rural-metro flows
Limitations in the digital/transport age — long-distance migration now cost-effective, weakening short-distance dominance
UPSC trap: Ravenstein said women migrate more than men for SHORT distances — often misquoted as overall higher female migration

concepts.name: Census Definition and Measurement of Migration in India
key_dimensions: Two Census methods: place of birth vs. place of last residence — each captures different migrant populations
'Duration of residence' categories (less than 1 year, 1–4 years, 5–9 years, 10+ years) and their policy use
Undercounting of migrants — reasons: temporary nature, no address proof, reluctance to register
UPSC trap: A person born in State A living in State B is a lifetime migrant by birth-method but may NOT appear in last-residence method if they returned briefly

concepts.name: Reasons for Migration: Gender Differentials
key_dimensions: Census data: women migrate predominantly for marriage (>60%), men for work/employment — implications for data interpretation
Marriage migration vs. associational migration (following spouse/family) — distinct phenomena often clubbed together
Female labour migration — emerging trend in garment, domestic work, ITES sectors — changing the traditional pattern
UPSC trap: High female migration in Census does NOT indicate female empowerment — it is largely marriage-driven, masking labour force exclusion

concepts.name: Inter-State Migration in India: Hotspots and Corridors
key_dimensions: Major sending states: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Odisha, Jharkhand — structural reasons for each
Major receiving states: Maharashtra, Delhi NCT, Gujarat, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu — sectoral demand analysis
Migration corridors — UP/Bihar to Delhi, Odisha to Surat (diamond industry), Northeast to metros (service sector)
UPSC trap: Kerala is both a major sender (Gulf migration) AND receiver (inter-state workers in construction/hospitality) — dual role

concepts.name: International Migration from India: Diaspora and Remittances
key_dimensions: Old vs. New diaspora — indentured labour (Fiji, Mauritius, Caribbean) vs. post-1947 skilled/unskilled migration
India as world's largest remittance receiver — World Bank data, top remittance-sending countries (UAE, USA, Saudi Arabia)
Brain drain vs. brain gain debate — skilled emigration loss to India vs. remittance and knowledge transfer gains
UPSC trap: Remittances are classified as PRIVATE transfers in Balance of Payments (Current Account), NOT capital flows — common error

concepts.name: Brain Drain: Causes, Consequences, and Policy Responses
key_dimensions: Sectors most affected: medicine, engineering, research — 'push' of poor research funding vs. 'pull' of global salaries
Economic cost to India: public investment in education not yielding domestic returns — fiscal externality concept
Brain gain counter-argument: returnee entrepreneurs (Silicon Valley–India corridor), diaspora philanthropy, technology transfer
Policy responses: VAJRA scheme, Global Indian Scientists and Technocrats (GIST), Pravasi Bharatiya Divas — evaluate effectiveness

concepts.name: Refugee vs. Migrant vs. Asylum Seeker: Legal Distinctions
key_dimensions: 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol definition of refugee — persecution on 5 specific grounds (race, religion, nationality, political opinion, social group)
India's position: NOT a signatory to 1951 Convention — implications for Rohingya, Tibetan, Sri Lankan Tamil treatment
Economic migrant vs. refugee — the policy trap: economic hardship does NOT qualify under Convention definition
UPSC trap: Stateless persons ≠ refugees automatically — statelessness and refugee status are separate legal categories (Rohingyas are both, but legally distinct)

concepts.name: Forced Migration: Climate-Induced and Disaster-Induced Displacement
key_dimensions: IDMC (Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre) data — India among top countries for disaster displacement annually
Climate migrants vs. environmental refugees — no legal status under international law for climate migrants
Slow-onset (sea-level rise, desertification) vs. sudden-onset (floods, cyclones) displacement — different policy needs
UPSC trap: 'Climate refugee' is NOT a legal term under international law — these persons have NO protected status under 1951 Convention

concepts.name: Impact of Migration on Source Regions
key_dimensions: Positive: remittance inflow, reduced pressure on land, skill acquisition by returnees, poverty alleviation
Negative: agricultural labour shortage during peak seasons, feminisation of agriculture, ageing rural population
Social impacts: breakdown of joint families, changing gender roles (women as de facto household heads), children's education disruption
UPSC trap: Remittances reduce poverty but can INCREASE inequality within villages — those with no migrant members fall further behind (relative deprivation)

concepts.name: Impact of Migration on Destination Cities: Opportunities and Challenges
key_dimensions: Labour supply benefits: migrants fill skill and wage gaps, especially in construction, domestic work, sanitation
Urban infrastructure stress: pressure on housing (slum formation), water, transport, schools, hospitals
Social tensions: nativist movements (Mumbai's 'Sons of Soil' — Shiv Sena), language-based discrimination, xenophobia
UPSC trap: Migrants are often portrayed as burden on cities — but evidence shows migrants are NET CONTRIBUTORS to urban GDP, not net consumers of welfare

concepts.name: Circular and Seasonal Migration: The Invisible Workforce
key_dimensions: Definition: repeated, short-duration movement between home and work — not captured well by Census (point-in-time survey)
Sectors: construction, brick kilns, sugarcane harvesting, salt pans — largely informal, contractual, piece-rate payment
Vulnerability profile: no social security, no voting rights at destination, no access to PDS/MGNREGS at destination
UPSC trap: Seasonal migrants are NOT covered under Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979 if employed through local contractors — a critical legal gap

concepts.name: Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1979 and Its Replacement
key_dimensions: Key provisions: registration of establishments, licensing of contractors, welfare obligations (wages, displacement allowance, housing)
Critical failures: poor implementation, 5-worker threshold excludes most migrants, no portability of benefits
Code on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions, 2020 — replaces the 1979 Act, lowers threshold, broader definition
UPSC trap: The 2020 Code is yet to be fully notified/implemented — be careful about 'current law' vs. 'proposed reform' in answers

concepts.name: COVID-19 Reverse Migration: Lessons for Migration Policy
key_dimensions: Scale: estimated 10–12 crore internal migrants returned home in 2020 — exposed invisibility of circular migrants in data and policy
Systemic failures revealed: no interstate portability of PDS, MGNREGS cards, health entitlements — welfare trapped at domicile
E-Shram Portal (2021) — first national database of unorganised workers including migrants — significance and limitations
UPSC trap: E-Shram registration does NOT automatically provide benefits — it is a database, not an entitlement scheme; benefits require separate programme linkage

concepts.name: Urbanisation and Migration Nexus: Agglomeration vs. Congestion
key_dimensions: Agglomeration economies: why migrants cluster in metros — network effects, job matching, knowledge spillovers (Jacobs externalities)
Congestion diseconomies: beyond a threshold, cities become inefficient — housing costs, commute time, pollution reduce productivity
Primate city problem in India — Delhi and Mumbai dominate, secondary cities underdeveloped — skewed migration magnet effect
UPSC trap: SMART Cities Mission does NOT aim to replace migration — it aims to develop 100 cities as liveable, but does NOT address root causes of distress migration

concepts.name: Demographic Dividend and Migration: Spatial Mismatch
key_dimensions: Young labour surplus in BIMARU states vs. ageing workforce in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Punjab — geographic mismatch
Migration as demographic equaliser — transfers labour from surplus to deficit regions, but requires skill matching
Risk of 'demographic dividend turning to disaster' if migration is distress-driven and destinations lack absorptive capacity
UPSC trap: States receiving migrants (Kerala, Punjab) are also states sending migrants abroad — they face simultaneous in-migration and out-migration at different skill levels

concepts.name: Transnational Migration and Its Socio-Cultural Impact
key_dimensions: Transnationalism: migrants maintaining simultaneous ties with origin and destination — dual identity, remittance economy, political engagement
Cultural remittances: migrants transferring values, consumption patterns, aspirations back home — rural modernisation and cultural disruption
Diaspora politics: Indian diaspora influencing bilateral relations (India-USA, India-Gulf), Pravasi Bharatiya Samman awards

UPSC trap: Transnationalism is different from assimilation — transnational migrants do NOT fully integrate into host society; this has different policy implications than classical immigrant integration models

concepts.name: Migration and Voting Rights: Electoral and Political Implications
key_dimensions: India's system: voter registration is domicile-based — migrants cannot vote at workplace; constituency interests of migrants unrepresented at destination
Remote voting proposal by Election Commission — EVMs for migrants — constitutional and logistical debates
Political representation gap: migrant-heavy constituencies in cities have voters registered elsewhere — leads to skewed local governance priorities
UPSC trap: NRI voting rights were granted in 2010 (Representation of People Amendment) but NRIs must be PHYSICALLY PRESENT in India to vote — no postal/proxy ballot for NRIs, unlike many democracies
